name: Korah
source_summary: A Levite who led a rebellion of 250 leaders against the authority of Moses and Aaron, claiming the whole congregation was equally holy; the earth opened and swallowed Korah and his household, and fire consumed the 250 who offered incense.
family_friendly_summary: Korah was a Levite who became jealous of Moses and Aaron's leadership. He gathered 250 respected leaders and challenged Moses, arguing that everyone in Israel was equally holy and that Moses and Aaron had no special right to lead. Moses proposed a test: everyone would offer incense before the LORD, and God would show clearly whom He had chosen. The ground opened up and swallowed Korah and his family, and fire consumed the 250 leaders who stood with him. It's a frightening story, but it shows how seriously God takes rebellion against the leaders and roles He has specifically appointed -- even as, remarkably, Korah's own descendants later became faithful worship leaders and psalm writers in Israel.
adult_story: Korah, a Levite of Kohath's family, led 250 prominent leaders of the congregation in open rebellion against Moses and Aaron, arguing, 'all the congregation are holy, every one of them... so why do you exalt yourselves?' (Numbers 16:1-3). Moses proposed a direct test before the LORD: Korah and his company would each bring a censer of incense the next day, and God would show whom He had chosen (16:5-7). Moses also confronted Korah specifically, pointing out that God had already given the Levites the high honor of tabernacle service, and that Korah's real complaint was against Aaron's priesthood, and ultimately against the LORD Himself (16:8-11). When the congregation gathered, God's glory appeared and threatened to consume the whole assembly, but Moses interceded for mercy on the general population (16:19-22). The ground then opened beneath Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their households, swallowing them alive into Sheol, while fire from the LORD consumed the 250 men who had offered incense (16:31-35). Their bronze censers were hammered into a covering for the altar as a lasting warning against unauthorized approach to God's presence (16:36-40). Remarkably, Korah's own line did not end with him -- 'the sons of Korah, however, did not die' (26:11), and his descendants became faithful gatekeepers and temple musicians generations later, credited as authors of several psalms (Psalm 42, 44-49, 84-85, 87-88) -- a rebellion answered with judgment on the man, yet mercy across his family line.
devotionals: Korah's rebellion against Aaron's priesthood was ultimately, Moses said, rebellion against the LORD Himself, and the ground opened beneath him as a lasting warning against approaching God on our own terms. Jesus alone opened a way to God that doesn't require seizing anything, because He is the way already given to us.

Though Korah died under judgment, Scripture notes 'the sons of Korah did not die,' and his descendants became temple musicians who wrote some of the Psalms. Jesus's mercy reaches past our worst family history the same way, so that judgment on one generation doesn't have to be the last word for the next.
